topic: the with statement and context managers

questions.question: Why should files usually be opened with the with statement?
questions.title: Using with open() Safely
questions.direct_answer: `with open(...)` closes the file when the block ends, including exceptional exits, so cleanup does not depend on every path remembering `close()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether `with` is understood as deterministic resource management rather than exception recovery.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying that `with` catches errors, or returning a handle that has already been closed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect block scope to explicit ownership and guaranteed release.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `open()` returns a file object that is also a context manager.
The name after `as` is usable only while the block owns the open resource.
Leaving the block closes the file on success or failure.
The `with` statement manages cleanup; it does not catch the exception.
After the block, file operations fail because the handle is closed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Files should normally be opened with `with` because a file handle is a resource that must be released on every exit path. `open()` returns a context manager. Entering the block produces the file object, and leaving it closes the handle whether the block finishes normally, returns, or raises an exception.

For example, a parser can use `with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:` and iterate over the lines. If conversion of one line raises `ValueError`, the file is still closed before that exception reaches the caller. The `with` statement does not swallow the failure; it guarantees cleanup around it. This is safer and clearer than placing `close()` at the bottom of a function, because that line is skipped by an early return or exception.

The file object should not be used after the block. Its `closed` attribute is true, and further reads or writes fail. If a function needs the content later, it should return the data, not the open handle. Manual `try` and `finally` can provide the same guarantee, but `with` is the standard concise form for objects that support the context-manager protocol.

sections.title: Ownership has a visible lifetime
sections.content:
The indentation of a `with` block shows exactly where the program owns the live resource. That visible lifetime is as important as automatic closure: readers can see that code outside the block cannot depend on the file remaining open.

Closing flushes Python's write buffers and releases the operating-system handle. Failing to close may delay data and can exhaust the process's available descriptors when many files are opened. The context manager makes cleanup deterministic rather than waiting for object destruction, whose timing should not be used as the program's resource policy.

If `open()` itself fails, no file has been entered and there is nothing for that context manager to close. If entry succeeds, Python guarantees its exit method is invoked when the block leaves.

sections.title: Resource lifetime
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Program
  participant F as File object
  P->>F: enter with block
  F-->>P: open handle
  P->>F: read or write
  Note over P,F: block may finish or raise
  P->>F: exit block
  F->>F: close and release handle
```

sections.title: Confirm closure after an exceptional exit
sections.content:
```python
from io import StringIO

stream = StringIO("10\nnot-a-number\n")
try:
    with stream as handle:
        values = [int(line) for line in handle]
except ValueError:
    pass

assert stream.closed is True
```

questions.question: How does the context manager protocol work in Python?
questions.title: Python Context Manager Protocol
questions.direct_answer: A context manager supplies `__enter__` and `__exit__`; `with` binds the enter result, runs the body, then calls exit with exception information if needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the actual protocol and its exception semantics are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the manager expression itself is always bound after `as`, or returning true accidentally.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain normal and exceptional exit paths and keep suppression explicit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `__enter__()` acquires or prepares the resource and returns the value bound after `as`.
`__exit__(type, value, traceback)` runs after the block on normal and exceptional exits.
On a normal exit, all three exception arguments are `None`.
A truthy `__exit__` return suppresses an exception; false or `None` lets it propagate.
`contextlib.contextmanager` expresses the same pattern with setup before `yield` and cleanup in `finally`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The context manager protocol consists of `__enter__` and `__exit__`. The `with` statement first evaluates the context expression and calls `__enter__`. Whatever `__enter__` returns is assigned to the optional name after `as`; it does not have to be the manager itself. Python then executes the block and calls `__exit__` when the block leaves.

If the block finishes normally, `__exit__` receives three `None` values. If the block raises, it receives the exception type, the exception object, and its traceback. Returning a false value, including `None`, allows that exception to continue. Returning a true value suppresses it, so suppression must be an intentional part of the manager's contract.

For example, a transaction manager can begin work in `__enter__`, then commit on a normal exit or roll back when exception information is present. A timer can record start and finish around the block without changing error behaviour. For simpler managers, `contextlib.contextmanager` uses a generator: setup goes before `yield`, the yielded value becomes the `as` target, and cleanup belongs in `finally` after the yield.

Once `__enter__` returns successfully, Python guarantees that `__exit__` is called. If acquisition fails inside `__enter__`, the block never starts, so that method must release anything it acquired only partially. The protocol packages a reusable setup-and-cleanup rule; it should release what it acquired and avoid hiding failures unless that is explicitly intended.

sections.title: The manager controls the boundary, not the body
sections.content:
A context manager does not decide which statements execute inside the block. It surrounds them with lifecycle behaviour. This separates resource policy from business logic and lets the same guarantee be reused wherever the manager appears.

Exception information makes transaction-style behaviour possible. The manager can inspect whether the body failed and choose rollback rather than commit. If cleanup itself fails, that new failure must be designed carefully because it can compete with the original exception. Resource release should therefore be small and dependable.

Generator-based managers must wrap `yield` in `try` and `finally`. An exception from the caller's block is raised at the yield point; without `finally`, cleanup statements after the yield may be skipped. Most such managers are single-use, so create them directly in each `with` statement.

sections.title: Protocol calls on both exits
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant W as with statement
  participant M as manager
  participant B as block
  W->>M: __enter__()
  M-->>W: value for as target
  W->>B: execute
  alt normal exit
    W->>M: __exit__(None, None, None)
  else exception
    W->>M: __exit__(type, value, traceback)
    M-->>W: false = propagate, true = suppress
  end
```

sections.title: Build a generator-based context manager
sections.content:
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

events = []

@contextmanager
def managed_label(name):
    events.append(f"open:{name}")
    try:
        yield name.upper()
    finally:
        events.append(f"close:{name}")

with managed_label("report") as label:
    assert label == "REPORT"
    events.append("use")

assert events == ["open:report", "use", "close:report"]
```
